sections.body:
A job interview is a conversation with a purpose. The interviewer already has your CV, your application and often a reference or an automated score. Their problem is not whether you exist. Their problem is whether you are the right person for this role, and they cannot decide that from a list of documents. The introduction is where you give them the shape of the answer in your own words.

So an introduction is not a biography and not a speech. It is a short, structured answer with three parts. First, **now**: who you are at this moment, in one sentence. Second, **before**: the experience that makes you relevant, in two or three sentences with one concrete result. Third, **next**: what you are looking for and why this company, in one sentence. Sixty to ninety seconds is enough. If you run past two minutes, the interviewer starts thinking about the schedule, not about you.

Notice what is missing. There is no life story, no list of every job you have had, no long description of your personality, and no summary of the company website. The interviewer has read the website. They want to know what only you can tell them.

Two other things are true at the same time. The introduction is your chance to set the frame: you decide which part of your experience the interviewer focuses on for the rest of the hour. And it is the one part of the interview you fully control. Questions can be hard, and answers can be cut short, but the opening is yours to prepare and yours to deliver.

The last point is why this article exists. Most candidates prepare answers to questions they cannot predict, and then improvise the introduction, which is the one thing that can be prepared in advance and improved by repetition. A calm, structured introduction also sets the tone for everything after it: it tells the interviewer that you can organise your thoughts under pressure, which is exactly the skill they are trying to judge.
examples: Good morning, my name is Linh Tran. I am a data analyst at a logistics company in Hai Phong, and I am here because your team is rebuilding its reporting system.
I have been in the field for six years, and last year I cut the monthly reporting time from three days to four hours.
What I am looking for now is a role where I own a product end to end.
sections.heading: What the introduction has to do

sections.body:
A reliable introduction is three short blocks. Learn them as three blocks and you will never run out of words in the silence after "Tell me about yourself".

The present. One or two sentences: your name, your current role, and the kind of work you do. Not your job title alone. Job titles are meaningless outside the company that invented them. "I am a customer operations officer" tells an interviewer something; "I am in charge of accounts" does not.

The past. Two or three sentences on the experience that matches the job you want. Choose one or two things rather than listing everything. The rule of thumb is: if it appears on your CV, say less about it, because they have read it. What they cannot read is what you did, how you did it and what changed because of it. Numbers are the shortest way to say this. "I reduced customer churn by 18 %" carries more weight than a full paragraph about being a team player.

The next. One sentence about why you want this job and what you want to do next. This is the part candidates skip, and it is the part that answers the question the interviewer is really asking, which is whether you will leave in four months. Mention the role, and if it is true, mention something specific about the company: a product, a market, a team, a piece of news. One sentence is enough. A speech about the company's history sounds like a speech.

Then stop. Do not ask the interviewer to tell you about the company. That is what the interview is for.

There is one more optional block, and it is useful when your CV looks thin in one area. You can add a single bridging sentence: "The part of my work closest to this role is the supplier side, which is why I moved from logistics into procurement two years ago." One bridge, placed in the past block, turns a gap into a deliberate step.
examples: I am a customer operations officer at a logistics company, and I look after twelve key accounts.
Before that I worked in warehouse scheduling, which is where I learned to work under tight deadlines.
Last year I introduced a first-line support process that reduced response time by 18 %.
I am looking for a role where I can lead a team and own a product.
sections.heading: The three parts, and how long each one is

sections.body:
Preparation is the whole job here. Give it twenty minutes and the words will be there when you need them.

Write the introduction out in full, then cut it. Most people write four paragraphs. Cut it to three blocks and no more than nine sentences. If it is longer, you will not say it faster in the room, you will just lose the ending.

Then say it aloud, standing up, at least five times. Reading it silently teaches your eyes, not your voice. The goal is not memorising a script. The goal is that each block has a fixed order and you can find the first sentence of each one under pressure.

Record the fourth attempt on your phone and listen to it. You will hear three things you never notice while speaking: how fast you go, whether you end every sentence upwards as if asking a question, and whether you say "um". Fix the fastest one first.

Finally, write a one-line reminder of your three keys. Three words on a card is enough. If your mind goes blank in the room, the card is the way back.
examples: My three keys are: operations, churn, procurement.
That is about a minute and a half. That is the right length.
sections.heading: How to prepare your introduction in five steps
steps: Write the introduction in three blocks: present, past, next.
Cut it to nine sentences or fewer.
Say it aloud, standing up, at least five times.
Record one attempt and listen for pace, tone and filler sounds.
Write three keywords on a card to jog your memory in the room.

sections.body:
Most interview answers are too general. "I am hard-working and a team player" is not a claim; it is a category, and every candidate is in it. The interviewer has no way to test it. Specifics are what they can test.

Use the **situation, task, action, result** pattern, in plain language. Say what the situation was, what you had to do, what you did, and what the outcome was. Four sentences is plenty. The pattern is famous because it stops people from describing a job instead of a result.

The result is the sentence that does the work. Give a number, a deadline, a reduction, a volume, a ranking, or a first-time event. "I handled accounts worth $4 million a year" is a result. "I improved the process" is a claim. If you genuinely cannot measure the result, describe the change instead: what was impossible before that became possible.

Use the past tense for what is finished and the present tense for what is still true. "I run the weekly reporting cycle" is present because you still do it. "I ran it for two years" is past because you do not. Interviewers notice this, and the wrong tense can make a current job sound like a job you have already left.

And do not describe your company; describe your work. "We are a leading provider of logistics solutions with 400 employees" tells the interviewer nothing, because every company says this. "We move about 300 containers a week between Hai Phong and Singapore" tells them what your work actually involved.

When you are asked about a weakness, do the same thing honestly and with a change attached. Name a real limitation, say what it cost you, and say what you did about it. That is a much better answer than a humblebrag such as "I work too hard", which everybody recognises as a way of refusing to answer.
examples: Three of our clients were losing shipments because nobody checked the manifests, so I built a checklist and trained the team on it.
After that, we lost two shipments in a quarter instead of one a month.
I am still responsible for that process today.
I sometimes take on too much at once, so I now agree the priority with my manager before I start.
sections.heading: How to describe your experience so that it counts

sections.body:
These are the terms that appear in almost every interview, and it helps to know them before you hear them.

A **CV** (curriculum vitae) is your written record of your education and work history. In the United States it is usually called a **résumé**. A **job description** is the document that lists the responsibilities of the role; read it before the interview and use its words.

A **hiring manager** is the person who needs the role filled and who usually decides. A **recruiter** finds and screens candidates. A **panel interview** has several interviewers taking questions, often one from each department. A **second interview** is a later round, usually with a more senior panel.

An **aptitude test** is a timed test of logic, numeracy or language. A **technical test** asks you to do a piece of work from the job, sometimes as a paid exercise. A **case study** gives you a business problem to analyse, common in consulting and management roles.

A **probation period** is a trial period at the start of a contract, often three or six months. A **notice period** is the time you must give before you leave a job, commonly one or two months. A **reference** is a person your employer may contact to check your history; in some countries it is a **reference check**, done with your consent.

Transferable skills are abilities that count in a new job even if the industry changes. **Stakeholders** are the people affected by a decision, inside or outside your organisation. **KPIs** are the numbers a role is measured by, short for key performance indicators.

And two words for the interview itself: **behavioural questions** ask what you did in the past, and **competency questions** ask which skill you used. Most behavioural questions follow one shape, and it is worth learning that shape before the room.
sections.heading: The words interviewers use, one by one

terms.example: I sent my CV and my cover letter on Monday morning.
terms.gloss: The document that lists your education and work history. In the United States it is usually called a résumé.

terms.example: The hiring manager asked me about the two projects I led last year.
terms.gloss: The person who needs the role filled and who usually makes the hiring decision.

terms.example: It was a panel interview, so I introduced myself briefly at the start.
terms.gloss: An interview with several interviewers at once, often one from each department of the company.

terms.example: The second stage was a numerical aptitude test with forty questions.
terms.gloss: A timed test of logic, numeracy or language, often given before or after the first interview.

terms.example: The contract starts with a three-month probation period.
terms.gloss: A trial period at the start of a contract, often three or six months, when either side can end the arrangement.

terms.example: I can give one month's notice, so I could start in April.
terms.gloss: The amount of time you must give before leaving a job, commonly one or two months.

terms.example: Could you give me a reference from your last manager?
terms.gloss: A person your former employer allows a new employer to contact to check your work history.

terms.example: Project coordination is a transferable skill, whatever the sector.
terms.gloss: An ability that counts in a new job even when the industry or the title is different.

terms.example: I had to keep three stakeholders updated without overloading them.
terms.gloss: Any person or group affected by a decision, inside or outside the organisation.

terms.example: That was a behavioural question, so she should give a real story, not a general principle.
terms.gloss: An interview question about something you actually did in the past, usually answered with a specific example.

sections.body:
Somewhere between the reception desk and the interview room there is a stretch of small talk. It is short, and it is not a test of your personality, but people form an impression in it anyway.

The most common opener is a comment about the journey or the building: "Did you have trouble finding the office?" The right answer is short and moves the conversation towards the work. "No trouble, I came by metro and the station is two minutes away, so I had a little time to look around." Then stop. Small talk ends when one person stops asking.

If the interviewer offers you water or coffee, accept it, and thank them once. If you are offered a choice of hot or cold, say which one rather than "whatever is fine" — small, clear preferences read better than politeness that sounds like indecision.

Some interviewers open with something slightly personal, usually about the role, the company or the weather. You can answer directly and briefly. You do not need a personal story, and you should not volunteer information about your health, your family or your salary. These are not impolite topics to raise, but they are not useful in the first two minutes either.

The one piece of small talk worth preparing is a single fact about the company or the sector that you can say without sounding like you copied it. "I read that you opened a second site last year" is fine. "Your mission statement is very inspiring" is not.

If you have a Vietnamese name, you will be asked how to pronounce it, and you will be asked what it means. Answer both, briefly, and then move on. "My name is Nguyen Thi Lan. It is pronounced like "Nwin Tey Lan", and the family name is Nguyen, which comes first." That answer takes five seconds and it often makes the interviewer more careful with your name for the rest of the hour.
examples: Did you have trouble finding the office? No, I came by metro and the station is close by.
My name is Nguyen Thi Lan. It is pronounced like "Nwin Tey Lan", and Nguyen is my family name.
I read that you opened a second warehouse last year, and I am curious how that changed the team.
Thank you, water is fine.
sections.heading: The small talk that comes before the questions

sections.body:
Badmouthing a former employer. Whether the boss was awful or the company was chaotic, the interviewer hears how you will speak about people you no longer work with. Say what you learned instead.

A prepared speech. If your introduction sounds recited, the interviewer stops listening. Deliver the content, not the script.

No numbers. "I improved customer service" could mean anything. One figure turns a claim into a result.

Arguing with the interviewer. If you disagree, disagree with the position, not the person. "I see it a different way, because in my last team the opposite approach worked." A candidate who argues well is remembered; a candidate who argues badly is not hired.

Asking about the salary first. It is your right to ask about pay, and it is legitimate later in the process. But in the first interview, in front of a panel, it reads as an interest in the money rather than the work.
sections.heading: Five things that cost candidates the job

sections.body:
Every serious interviewer ends an interview by asking what questions you have. Candidates who say "no, thank you" lose a free chance to show preparation.

Prepare three questions and ask two or three of them. Three categories work well.

Questions about the role show you have read the job description. "From the job description, it looks like the first six months are focused on the migration. Is that still the plan?" A question that shows you read the description is worth more than a generic one.

Questions about the team show you are thinking about how work actually happens. "How is the work split between your team and the engineers in Hanoi?" or "What does a good first three months look like in this role?" The second one is a strong question, because it signals that you intend to do the job well.

Questions about the organisation show you think beyond your own desk. "What is the biggest problem this team is trying to solve this year?"

Ask one question about how success is measured: "How will you know, in six months, that I did well in this role?" It is professional, it is specific, and it usually produces a good answer.

Avoid questions that make the interviewer defensive: questions about overtime that sound like complaints, questions about the previous employee, questions about why the last person left, and anything that only asks about perks in the first meeting. If you want to know about pay, ask at the right stage: "Can you tell me the salary range for this role?" is fine in a first call with a recruiter, and better once the company has shown interest.

And note down the names of the people you meet. Sending a follow-up email that names them is far better than one that says "Dear Hiring Manager".
examples: What does a good first three months look like in this role?
How will you know, in six months, that I did well?
From the job description, it looks like the first six months focus on the migration. Is that still the plan?
What is the biggest challenge this team is trying to solve this year?
sections.heading: Questions to ask at the end

sections.body:
The last two minutes decide how the interview is remembered. The interviewer has a stack of notes and is about to write something down, so what you say at the end is what gets written.

Summarise briefly. Two sentences: your strongest point and your interest. "Thank you for your time. I have really enjoyed hearing how the team works, and I would be glad to bring my operations experience to the reporting side of the role." This is not begging, and it is not repeating the introduction. It is a closing statement, and it gives the interviewer a ready-made summary to write down.

Then thank them by name: "Thank you, Ms Nguyen. I appreciate the time you took today." Stand up, shake hands if that is what happens in this workplace, and leave when you are told to leave.

Do not ask for the result in the room. "When will I hear from you?" is a question about their process, and it is better asked by email. Asking in the room puts the interviewer on the spot and rarely produces a date.

Two practical details. Take the contact details of the recruiter, and write down the name of every person you met as you leave the room, while it is still fresh. If there is a second stage, ask what it involves: "What is the next step in the process, and when should I expect to hear about it?" is a normal question, and a good one to ask before you stand up.

Finally, expect silence on the way out. The interviewer may walk you to the lift and say nothing more, and that is normal. Do not fill the silence with a joke about the interview.
examples: Thank you for your time. I have really enjoyed hearing how the team works, and I would be glad to bring my experience to this role.
Thank you, Mr Tran. I appreciate the time you took today.
What is the next step in the process, and when should I expect to hear about it?
Could I have your email address, so I can send the documents you asked for?
sections.heading: How to close the interview well

sections.body:
Send a short thank-you email. It takes ten minutes, and many interviewers say plainly that it makes a difference.

Send it the same day or the next morning. A week later it looks like an afterthought. Keep it under 150 words. It should have three parts: thanks, one specific thing from the conversation, and one sentence about your interest.

The specific part is what makes it work. "Thank you for explaining how the reporting cycle works in your team" is memorable. "Thank you for your time and for considering my application" is generic, and it is the same email you sent to the last company.

Keep the subject line simple and professional: "Thank you — [Job title] interview", or "Follow-up from my interview on [date]". Do not use an exclamation mark unless you have a real relationship with the reader.

Close with a clear next step. If they asked for a document, attach it and say so. If you are still interested, say so: "I remain very interested in the role and would be glad to provide anything else you need." If you are no longer interested, this is also the moment to withdraw politely, which saves everyone time.

Do not ask for a decision in the follow-up email, and do not write more than one paragraph of gratitude. If you sent a document, confirm exactly what you sent. If you do not hear back within a week, one polite follow-up is acceptable: "I wanted to check that you received my portfolio on Monday."

One habit worth keeping: keep a copy of every email you send after an interview, with the date and the name of the role. When you are asked three months later why you did not hear from a company, you will be able to answer precisely.
examples: Subject: Thank you — Data Analyst interview
Thank you for the time you gave me on Tuesday, and for explaining how the reporting cycle works in your team.
I have attached the sample dashboard you asked for. I remain very interested in the role.
I wanted to check that you received my portfolio on Monday.
sections.heading: The follow-up email after the interview

item.summary: An interview introduction is not a biography. It is a short, structured answer that tells the interviewer who you are, why you are relevant and what you want next. After reading this you can prepare a 60-second introduction, describe your experience with evidence, ask questions that show judgement, and close the interview and follow up in a way that is remembered.
item.title: How to Introduce Yourself in a Job Interview
